title: Why Reformed definitions of justifying faith diverge — omit the common, mark the difference
source_text: LXXXIII. Supra quoque docuimus fidem justificantem a Reformatis pluribus & discrepantibus modis describi atque definiri. Quae discrepantia inde primo oritur, quod multi in sua definitione omittunt id quod fides justificans commune habet cum fide historica: & solum notare volunt id quo fides justificans ab historica differt. Ut qui in sua definitione mentionem non faciunt assensus quem fides justificans praebet toti Verbo Dei ipsi revelato atque proposito. Deinde sunt qui fidem justificantem ab una proprietate, alii vero qui ab alia describunt.
pass_a_gloss: Above we have also taught that justifying faith is described and defined by the Reformed in many and discrepant ways. Which discrepancy arises first from this, that many in their definition omit that which justifying faith has in common with historical faith: and wish only to note that by which justifying faith differs from historical. As those who in their definition make no mention of the assent which justifying faith gives to the whole Word of God itself revealed and proposed. Then there are those who describe justifying faith from one property, but others from another.
pass_b_english: Reformed definitions of justifying faith diverge for two reasons.
First: many omit what it shares with historical faith and mark only the difference — so they skip the assent justifying faith still gives to the whole revealed Word.
Second: some define from one property, others from another.
